- To prevent decompression sickness ('the bends'), astronauts perform a pre-breathe protocol by inhaling 100% oxygen to purge dissolved nitrogen from body tissues. [F-003]
- To reduce pre-breathe times and facilitate lunar surface extravehicular activities (EVAs), the atmosphere in lunar habitats and pressurized rovers is anticipated to have pressure and oxygen concentration intermediate between spacesuits and Earth sea-level atmosphere. [F-004]
- The intermediate atmosphere for lunar operations is anticipated to feature an oxygen concentration of 30% or higher, with a total pressure of 10.2 psi or lower. [F-005]
- According to the challenge text, this represents more than a 40% increase in oxygen concentration compared to Earth's atmosphere, substantially increasing material flammability. [F-006]
- In free fall, buoyancy-driven natural convection and buoyant rise of hot exhaust gases are absent, causing flames to behave dramatically differently from terrestrial flames; for example, a candle flame becomes a dim blue, spherical diffusion flame. [F-008]

facts.claim: To prevent decompression sickness ('the bends'), astronauts perform a pre-breathe protocol by inhaling 100% oxygen to purge dissolved nitrogen from body tissues.

To reduce pre-breathe times and facilitate lunar surface extravehicular activities (EVAs), the atmosphere in lunar habitats and pressurized rovers is anticipated to have pressure and oxygen concentration intermediate between spacesuits and Earth sea-level atmosphere.
The intermediate atmosphere for lunar operations is anticipated to feature an oxygen concentration of 30% or higher, with a total pressure of 10.2 psi or lower.
According to the challenge text, this represents more than a 40% increase in oxygen concentration compared to Earth's atmosphere, substantially increasing material flammability.

In free fall, buoyancy-driven natural convection and buoyant rise of hot exhaust gases are absent, causing flames to behave dramatically differently from terrestrial flames; for example, a candle flame becomes a dim blue, spherical diffusion flame.

fields.name: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (Saffire-II)
fields.fuel_material: silicone sheet (2-1…2-4) | SIBAL fabric (2-5, 2-6) | PMMA + Nomex (2-7) | structured and flat PMMA (2-8, 2-9)
fields.fuel_shape_size: 9 thin flat strips, each 50 mm × 290 mm; thickness 0.27-1.03 mm (silicone), 0.37 mm (SIBAL), 0.85 + 0.37 mm (PMMA+Nomex), 10 mm (PMMA)
fields.o2_note: derived from CO2 production, referenced to the ISS initial O2 (PSI-99 Note 1); the CSV 2-1 value (21.5) was excluded — see the conflict list
fields.flow_note: the PSI-99 CSV gives 20 cm/s for 2-6; the pre-flight plan gives 30 cm/s for S6/S9 — 20-25 chosen
fields.hardware: other: Saffire flow unit with a 9-sample card (inside Cygnus, after unberthing from the ISS; not MSG/CIR)
fields.lunar_note: O2 upper bound and/or pressure lower bound unknown
fields.main_finding: None of the four silicone samples burned significantly in microgravity, and the source states that silicone flammability in microgravity appears reduced compared with 1-g at the flows tested; the 5 cm SIBAL strips burned completely (2.1 mm/s at 20 cm/s, 2.6 mm/s at 25 cm/s), while Nomex did not ignite despite the PMMA pilot flame.

[Saffire-I, Saffire-II, Saffire-III | S-022: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety (Saffire I-III Results) | Introduction]
Introduction
• Despite millennia of experience with fire, over 3,000 people die from fires each
year in the U.S. • Fire is a catastrophic hazard for spacecraft
• However, without any empirical results, it is impossible to be sure that our
predictions of fire behavior in a spacecraft are realistic. • What will kill you first? • CO buildup? • Other toxic products? • Heat? • Smoke? • Pressure Rise? • How should the crew respond? All inhabited types of structure, vehicle, or even
open space on earth have been the subject of
full scale fire studies and/or training.

[Saffire-I, Saffire-II, Saffire-III | S-022: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety (Saffire I-III Results) | Far Field Diagnostics]
Forward Steps
• The Saffire experiments were the first practical-scale spacecraft fire safety
investigations. • In addition to pioneering a new research capability, they determined that
concurrent flames can achieve a steady spread rate and that overall the
concurrent spread rates are strongly influenced the the flow duct size. • The next Saffire series will examine larger fires of longer duration to
examine the impact of a fire on the vehicle habitability .

[Saffire-I, Saffire-II, Saffire-III | S-022: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety (Saffire I-III Results) | Objectives:]
Objectives:
♦ Demonstrate spacecraft fire monitoring and cleanup
technologies in a realistic spacecraft fire scenario
♦ Characterize fire growth in high O , low pressure atmospheres
♦ Provide data to validate models of prediction of the
impact of a fire on vehicle habitability

[Saffire-I, Saffire-II, Saffire-III | S-021: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status | 2.1 Sample Materials]
2.1 Sample Materials
The sample material for Saffire-I and III is a composite
fabric consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate
(75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight). It is called
SIBAL cloth because it was developed for the Solid
Inflammability Boundary at Low-Speeds (SIBAL)
spaceflight experiment and has been used in many space
experiments because it burns like cotton but maintains
structural integrity after the cotton is consumed. The
objective of the Saffire-I and III tests will be to

rules.rule: Do NOT extrapolate microgravity results directly to Lunar or Martian gravity without explicitly stating the lack of direct partial-gravity empirical data and explaining bounding logic ([F-019], [F-021]).

When queried regarding combustion in Lunar or Martian gravity, explicitly clarify that NASA PSI currently contains no partial-gravity test data [F-019]. Mention E-FIELD electric field chemi-ion simulation [F-020] and 0-g/1-g bounding methodology [F-021] if relevant.

Never assess spacecraft fire flammability solely on oxygen percentage. Always evaluate oxygen partial pressure (via calculation), total pressure, diluent inert species (N2, CO2, He), and ventilation forced flow velocity together.
If asked about rocket engine or thruster propellant fires, clearly state that propulsion systems are outside the scope of PSI microgravity science due to momentum-dominated flow regimes [F-022].

For every experimental finding reported, cite the exact test conditions: fuel type, geometry, oxygen concentration, ambient pressure, flow velocity, and hardware facility. If a condition is omitted in the source, label it as 'unspecified'; do NOT guess.
If an empirical value or data point is absent from the indexed chunks and Golden Table, state 'data not available in repository'. Never fabricate numerical values from LLM parametric memory.
When source documents report conflicting findings or values, present both sources with their respective document citations, PI names, and publication years; do not arbitrarily select one.

Clearly distinguish between empirical flight experiment findings (PSI / peer-reviewed reports), challenge guidelines, mathematical derivations, and speculative engineering hypotheses. Never present interpretation as an empirical fact.
